course.title: AP U.S. History
course.description: Trace how Americans have argued over identity, power, work, and their place in the world, from the societies that existed before 1491 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Follow the nation's development from early contact and colonization through independence, civil war, industrialization, world wars, and recent decades.

unit.title: Period 2
unit.description: Follow the Spanish, French, Dutch, and British colonies, the regions of British North America, Atlantic trade, slavery, and colonial society from 1607 to 1754.

framework.name: Course themes
framework.title: Use the course themes to choose your evidence
framework.intro: The themes connect developments across all nine periods. A piece of evidence can fit more than one theme; choose the one that answers the prompt.
framework.sourceNote: Theme names, codes, and descriptions follow the AP U.S. History Course and Exam Description (fall 2026).

themes.title: American and National Identity
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why definitions of American and national identity and values have developed among the diverse and changing population of North America as well as on related topics, such as citizenship, constitutionalism, foreign policy, assimilation, and American exceptionalism.
themes.question: Who counted as American, and what did people believe the nation stood for?
themes.example: Debates over ratifying the Constitution turned on what kind of republic Americans wanted.

themes.title: Work, Exchange, and Technology
themes.description: This theme focuses on the factors behind the development of systems of economic exchange, particularly the role of technology, economic markets, and government.
themes.question: How did people earn a living, trade, and use new technology?
themes.example: Canals and railroads tied farmers in the West to markets in the East.

themes.title: Geography and the Environment
themes.description: This theme focuses on the role of geography and both the natural and human-made environments in the social and political developments in what would become the United States.
themes.question: How did land, climate, and resources shape choices, and how did people change them?
themes.example: The Chesapeake's climate suited tobacco, which shaped its labor system.

themes.title: Migration and Settlement
themes.description: This theme focuses on why and how the various people who moved to and within the United States both adapted to and transformed their new social and physical environments.
themes.question: Why did people move, and how did they change the places they settled?
themes.example: The Great Migration brought African Americans from the rural South to northern cities.

themes.title: Politics and Power
themes.description: This theme focuses on how different social and political groups have influenced society and government in the United States as well as how political beliefs and institutions have changed over time.
themes.question: Who held power, how did they use it, and who challenged it?
themes.example: The New Deal expanded the federal government's role in the economy.

themes.title: America in the World
themes.description: This theme focuses on the interactions between nations that affected North American history in the colonial period and on the influence of the United States on world affairs.
themes.question: How did contact, trade, diplomacy, and war connect America to other nations?
themes.example: The Seven Years' War left Britain in debt and changed its policies toward the colonies.

themes.title: American and Regional Culture
themes.description: This theme focuses on the how and why national, regional, and group cultures developed and changed as well as how culture has shaped government policy and the economy.
themes.question: How did beliefs, religion, arts, and media develop and shape public life?
themes.example: The Second Great Awakening inspired many Americans to join reform movements.

themes.title: Social Structures
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why systems of social organization develop and change as well as the impact that these systems have on the broader society.
themes.question: How were people ranked by race, class, and gender, and how did that change?
themes.example: The growth of a middle class in the Gilded Age changed ideas about leisure and family.

questions.prompt: A student wants to write a strong comparison of Spanish and English colonization. Which approach would be most effective?
choices: Describe everything known about Spanish colonies, then everything known about English colonies
List the founding dates of colonies in each empire and arrange them in chronological order
Choose a criterion such as labor, then explain a similarity, a difference, and the reasons for them
Argue that one empire's colonies were better than the other's and give examples of success
questions.explanation: A strong comparison uses a criterion, names a similarity and a difference, and explains why they existed.
choiceExplanations: Describing each subject separately is description and not comparison.
A list of dates is not a comparison.
A strong comparison uses a criterion, names a similarity and a difference, and explains why they existed.
A comparison explains similarities and differences instead of judging which is better.
questions.distinguisher: Describing each empire in turn feels thorough, but it never connects the two.
questions.subskillText: Identify patterns among or connections between historical developments and processes.

questions.prompt: Why does a strong comparison include a criterion?
choices: It ensures that both developments are measured against the same standard of comparison
It allows the writer to avoid discussing differences between the two developments being compared
It requires the writer to discuss only the causes of each development and not the effects
It limits the comparison to events that happened in a single year or a single colony
questions.explanation: A criterion, such as labor or religion, gives both subjects a common standard so that their similarities and differences can be judged fairly.
choiceExplanations: A criterion, such as labor or religion, gives both subjects a common standard so that their similarities and differences can be judged fairly.
A comparison must include differences as well as similarities.
A criterion can be any shared feature, such as labor or religion.
A criterion does not limit a comparison to one year or place.
questions.distinguisher: A criterion focuses the comparison, but it does not allow the writer to skip differences.
questions.subskillText: Identify patterns among or connections between historical developments and processes.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a difference between French and Spanish relations with American Indians?
choices: The French relied on trade alliances and intermarriage, while the Spanish subjugated and converted Native peoples
The French subjugated and converted Native peoples, while the Spanish relied on trade alliances and intermarriage
The French avoided contact with Native peoples, while the Spanish traded with them for furs and deerskins
The French forced Native peoples to work in mines, while the Spanish never required Native labor
questions.explanation: French colonies depended on trade alliances and intermarriage for furs, while Spanish colonies built institutions based on subjugation and conversion.
choiceExplanations: French colonies depended on trade alliances and intermarriage for furs, while Spanish colonies built institutions based on subjugation and conversion.
This reverses the two empires' methods.
The French depended on contact with Native peoples for furs.
The Spanish used Native labor extensively.
questions.distinguisher: The reversed statement uses the right ideas for the wrong empires.
questions.subskillText: Identify patterns among or connections between historical developments and processes.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best explains why relations with American Indians differed in French and English colonies?
choices: French colonists were Catholic and English colonists were Protestant, so they could not trade together
Colonies built around the fur trade needed Native partners, while farming colonies needed Native land
The French government banned its colonists from settling on farms, while England required them to farm
English colonists lived among Native peoples in shared villages, while French colonists lived apart
questions.explanation: Colonists who relied on furs depended on Native partners, but colonists who relied on farming wanted Native land.
choiceExplanations: Religion did not prevent trade, and the main difference lay in each colony's economic goals.
Colonists who relied on furs depended on Native partners, but colonists who relied on farming wanted Native land.
No government rule explains the difference.
English colonists lived separately from Native peoples.
questions.distinguisher: Religion differed between the empires, but the economic purpose of each colony better explains its relations with Native peoples.
questions.subskillText: Explain how a historical development or process relates to another historical development or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following was a similarity among all of the British colonial regions?
choices: Each developed elected assemblies and took part in trade across the Atlantic
Each relied mainly on enslaved Africans for its labor and exported a single crop
Each was governed directly by Parliament through officials chosen and paid in London
Each was settled almost entirely by English Puritans seeking religious uniformity
questions.explanation: All of the regions built elected assemblies, traded across the Atlantic, and became more English over time.
choiceExplanations: All of the regions built elected assemblies, traded across the Atlantic, and became more English over time.
New England and the middle colonies relied mainly on family farms.
The colonies developed their own assemblies and local government.
The colonies were settled by many groups, and the middle colonies were diverse.
questions.distinguisher: Slavery existed in every colony to some degree, but it was not the main labor system in all of them.
questions.subskillText: Identify patterns among or connections between historical developments and processes.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best explains why plantation colonies relied on large enslaved workforces while New England did not?
choices: New England colonists were forbidden by law from owning enslaved people, but plantation colonists were not
New England colonists had a steady supply of indentured servants, but plantation colonists had none
Plantation colonists lived in towns with town meetings that encouraged them to rely on enslaved labor
Long growing seasons favored labor-intensive cash crops, while rocky soil favored family farms
questions.explanation: Environment shaped the economies, since a long growing season made large cash-crop plantations profitable and New England's soil favored smaller farms.
choiceExplanations: Slavery was legal in New England.
Planters in the Chesapeake also used indentured servants before turning to enslaved Africans.
Town meetings were a New England institution, and plantation colonists lived on dispersed estates.
Environment shaped the economies, since a long growing season made large cash-crop plantations profitable and New England's soil favored smaller farms.
questions.distinguisher: Slavery existed in New England, but its farms were too small to use many enslaved laborers.
questions.subskillText: Explain how a historical development or process relates to another historical development or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following was a difference between New England and the middle colonies?
choices: New England was more ethnically and religiously diverse and exported tobacco and rice
The middle colonies were settled mostly by English Puritans and had no elected assemblies
New England relied on enslaved Africans for most labor, while the middle colonies did not
The middle colonies were more ethnically and religiously diverse and exported grain
questions.explanation: Fertile land and trade attracted many kinds of settlers to the middle colonies, which exported wheat and flour, while New England was more uniformly English and Puritan.
choiceExplanations: This reverses the regions' diversity and ignores their actual exports.
Puritans settled New England, and the middle colonies had assemblies.
New England's small farms used relatively few enslaved laborers.
Fertile land and trade attracted many kinds of settlers to the middle colonies, which exported wheat and flour, while New England was more uniformly English and Puritan.
questions.distinguisher: The reversed statement is wrong on both diversity and exports.
questions.subskillText: Identify patterns among or connections between historical developments and processes.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a similarity between the British and Dutch colonies in North America?
choices: Both were settled mainly by large numbers of families who farmed land taken from Native peoples
Both were governed mainly by missionaries who sought to convert Native peoples to Christianity
Both were founded with the backing of private companies that hoped to earn profits
Both relied mainly on a Native labor draft similar to the encomienda system used by the Spanish
questions.explanation: The Virginia Company financed Jamestown, and the Dutch West India Company organized New Netherland, so private companies backed both.
choiceExplanations: The Dutch colony had relatively few Europeans and relied on trade.
Neither colony was governed mainly by missionaries.
The Virginia Company financed Jamestown, and the Dutch West India Company organized New Netherland, so private companies backed both.
The encomienda was a Spanish system.
questions.distinguisher: The family-farm choice describes the English pattern but not the Dutch one.
questions.subskillText: Identify patterns among or connections between historical developments and processes.
